planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Albomarginata is one of the oldest and most vigorous hosta cultivars in cultivation and bulks up into a full clump within a few seasons.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely planted hosta cultivars in American gardens, Albomarginata forms a dense, symmetrical mound of oval, medium-green leaves edged with a crisp, narrow white-to-cream margin. It is exceptionally vigorous and tolerant of a wide range of shade conditions, multiplying steadily into a full-size clump within just a few seasons, which is why it has long been a mainstay foundation planting and mass-edging choice at garden centers. Pale lavender, funnel-shaped flowers rise on tall scapes in mid-summer above the foliage. Because it holds its variegation and vigor reliably even in less-than-ideal soil, it remains a benchmark starter hosta against which showier modern cultivars are often compared.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Honeybells is a fast, easy old-fashioned hybrid grown chiefly for its powerfully fragrant summer flowers.

directions: Honeybells is a fast-growing, old-fashioned hosta hybrid prized above all for its powerfully sweet-scented, near-white to pale lavender flowers that open in late summer, a trait inherited from its Hosta plantaginea parentage. The light yellow-green, glossy, wavy-edged leaves are thinner-substanced and less refined than modern cultivars, but the plant's rapid growth and generous flowering make it a long-time garden-center staple for gardeners who want fragrance near a porch, path, or window. It multiplies quickly into a large, casual mound and tolerates more morning sun than most blue or gold hostas without losing vigor. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain flowering performance.

common_name: Sugar and Cream Hosta (Fragrant White-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Sugar and Cream is a variegated sport of the fragrant cultivar Honeybells and shares its parent's fast growth and flower fragrance.

directions: Sugar and Cream is a variegated sport of the classic fragrant hosta Honeybells, combining the same sweetly scented, near-white summer flowers with broad, creamy-white leaf margins surrounding a light-green center. The wavy, glossy leaves brighten as the season progresses, and the plant shares its parent's fast growth rate and tolerance of somewhat more sun than typical shade hostas, provided soil moisture stays consistent. Its combination of showy variegation and strong fragrance makes it a popular choice for foundation plantings and mixed shade borders near seating areas. Established clumps flower reliably from mid to late summer on tall scapes held well above the foliage.

common_name: Silver Threads and Golden Needles Hosta (Narrow-Leaf Fountain Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this narrow-leaved novelty hosta forms an upright, grass-like clump rather than a typical spreading mound.

directions: Unlike typical broad-leaved hostas, Silver Threads and Golden Needles forms an upright, fountain-like clump of extremely narrow, almost grass-like lance leaves with a gold-green center and a fine, irregular creamy-white margin. The slender foliage gives the plant a distinctly different silhouette from rounded or heart-shaped hosta cultivars, making it useful as a textural accent or ornamental-grass substitute in shaded plantings. It is a modest, slow spreader that keeps a tidy, self-contained clump rather than sprawling widely. Pale lavender flowers appear on slender scapes in summer, complementing the plant's fine-textured overall look.

common_name: Chinese Sunrise Hosta (Gold Leaf Red-Petiole Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a few hours of morning sun to partial shade; Chinese Sunrise is a Q&Z Nursery gold-leaf introduction grown for its color-changing foliage and red-tinted stems.

directions: Chinese Sunrise, a Q&Z Nursery introduction, is grown chiefly for its vivid color contrast: broad, corrugated gold leaves emerge chartreuse in spring and deepen to bright gold by summer, set off dramatically against bright red-tinted petioles and lower stems. The upright, vase-shaped clump displays the colorful stems prominently beneath the foliage canopy, a feature most other gold hostas lack. It holds its gold color best with a few hours of morning sun, while afternoon shade prevents leaf scorch in hotter climates. Pale lavender flowers appear in mid to late summer on scapes that echo the red stem coloring.

common_name: Gypsy Rose Hosta (Blue Leaf Red-Petiole Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gypsy Rose was bred by Hans Hansen as part of his red-petiole hosta line and holds its blue leaf color best out of direct sun.

directions: Bred by Hans Hansen as part of his red-petiole hosta breeding line, Gypsy Rose pairs thick, rounded, blue-green leaves with strikingly vivid burgundy-red petioles and stem bases that stay colorful all season rather than fading by midsummer as in many older red-stemmed hostas. The heavy leaf substance gives it above-average slug resistance, and the contrast between the cool blue foliage and hot-red stems makes it a standout specimen or focal point in a shade bed. It forms a dense, symmetrical mound and holds its blue leaf color best in fuller shade, since direct sun fades the waxy blue bloom on the foliage. Lavender flowers appear on red-tinted scapes in summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun; Hanky Panky is a Q&Z Nursery sport with an unusual reverse-variegated leaf pattern.

directions: Hanky Panky is a Q&Z Nursery sport notable for its reverse variegation pattern, an irregular creamy-white leaf center bordered by a wide, dark blue-green margin, the opposite arrangement of most white-centered hostas. This gives the clump strong visual presence at a distance despite bearing thick, substantial leaves more typical of solid-colored cultivars. Because so much leaf tissue lacks chlorophyll, it grows a bit more slowly than all-green sports and benefits from consistent moisture and protection from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the white centers. Lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in summer above the rounded, cupped foliage.

common_name: Mighty Mouse Hosta (Vigorous Mouse Ears Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mighty Mouse is a Hans Hansen introduction from the mouse-ears breeding group, larger and more vigorous than Blue Mouse Ears.

directions: Bred by Hans Hansen as part of the popular mouse-ears group of miniature to small hostas, Mighty Mouse offers the same thick, rounded, powdery blue-green leaves and compact, cupped growth habit as its parent Blue Mouse Ears but grows noticeably larger and more vigorously, filling in a fuller clump in less time. The heavy leaf substance provides good resistance to slug damage and helps the foliage hold its blue color through summer heat better than thinner-leaved cultivars. Its intermediate size fills the gap between true miniature hostas and full-size landscape cultivars, working well along path edges or in mixed containers. Lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, held just above the foliage.
